intro_title_en: Start with no Chinese: script and chapter preparation
intro_en: Start here with no Chinese assumed. Read the script preparation for your next chapter before its story. If you arrived through a direct chapter link, use How to read to return here first. The preparation is additional to the chapter, its Pensa and its workbook. You can study it in several short sittings.

Read the Chinese horizontally from left to right. A square written form is a character; a word can contain one or more characters. The story has no spaces between its ordinary words. Punctuation separates clauses and speech. Learn the traditional forms shown here; no simplified-script knowledge is assumed.

Roman letters give modern Mandarin citation readings, not reconstructed ancient sounds. A tone mark belongs to the syllable: ā is high and level, á rises, ǎ dips and rises in isolation, à falls. An unmarked syllable is light. Citation tones may change in connected speech. Keep your tongue as for “ee” and round your lips for ü. Xī'ān has two syllables, xī plus ān; xiān is one syllable. You will answer in Chinese characters, without tone-typing or audio tasks.

For typed answers, a traditional-Chinese pinyin input method lets you type the supplied roman reading without tone marks, then choose the exact written character from its candidates. Compare shapes carefully. While learning input, you can copy a form from the visible reference. Pinyin is a lookup aid; its letters do not all have English sound values, and fluent Mandarin pronunciation is not a prerequisite for following these scenes.

A subject is the person or thing a sentence says something about. In the worked examples a person performs an action on a book: the book is the object directly related to that action. Verbs do not take English-style person or tense endings. No word for “a” or “the” is needed in these examples.

Chapter 1: study only these packets now. Learn each form with its meaning; compare the shapes; try each cue before looking at the answer-check paragraph. Use the reference first, then cover it for another attempt. Answer paragraphs are checks, not extra narrative reading.
Chapter 1, packet 1. New forms:
人 — rén — person.
書 — shū — book; written document.
持 — chí — hold; carry.
取 — qǔ — take.
人持書。 — A person holds a book.
人取書。 — A person takes a book.
Attempt 1. The object being carried is a bound text. Supply its written name: ___ Reference: 人 · 取 · 持 · 書
Attempt 2. Supply the action meaning “take”, rather than keep holding: ___ Reference: 人 · 取 · 持 · 書
Attempt 3. Supply the word for the person, rather than the object carried: ___ Reference: 人 · 取 · 持 · 書
Attempt 4. The book remains in someone’s hands. Supply “hold/carry”: ___ Reference: 人 · 取 · 持 · 書
Attempt 5. From the reference, retrieve the expression for a book rather than a human being: ___ Reference: 人 · 取 · 持 · 書
Attempt 6. The participant who takes the book is a person. Supply that participant word: ___ Reference: 人 · 取 · 持 · 書
Check after attempting: 書 · 取 · 人 · 持 · 書 · 人.
Chapter 1, packet 2. New forms:
安 — Ān — An (novice copyist).
門 — mén — doorway; gate.
入 — rù — enter.
出 — chū — go out.
人 / 入 — These similar strokes join differently. Compare the upper joins and link each form to its own meaning; do not treat them as interchangeable.
Attempt 1. An goes out through the doorway; supply “go out”, not “enter”. 安___門。 Reference: 持 · 出 · 安 · 入 · 取 · 門
Attempt 2. An enters through a doorway; supply the place word. 安入___。 Reference: 持 · 出 · 安 · 入 · 取 · 門
Attempt 3. Choose the expression that means “An (novice copyist)”, then cover the reference and write it: ___ Reference: 持 · 出 · 安 · 入 · 取 · 門

一 — yī — one.
二 — èr — two.
坐 — zuò — sit.
大 — dà — large.
一 / 二 — Count the separate horizontal strokes: the forms encode different quantities.

In the bounded book-counting examples, the numeral directly precedes the noun: no extra counting word is needed here. Large and small also precede the noun they describe. Broader quantity patterns come later.

Check after attempting: 坐 · 一 · 二 · 大 · 入 · 出.

Chapter 1, packet 6. New forms:
視 — shì — look at.
還 — huán — return.

Attempt 1. An opens the doorway; supply “open”, not “close”. 安___門。 Reference: 見 · 還 · 閉 · 視 · 開 · 立

Chapter 2, packet 2. New forms:

Attempt 2. Identify which reference expression has this meaning, without following reference order: “few; little”. ___ Reference: 字 · 少 · 多 · 開 · 閉 · 帙

Chapter 2, packet 3. New forms:
有 — yǒu — have; there is.
無 — wú — not have; there is no.
異 — yì — different.
破 — pò — be broken.
Construction preparation: finish the form cards, then follow this familiar action scene before adding the new pattern. 安持大書，寧持小書。安取一書，寧持一書。人開門，安見人。安坐，寧立。

Put the person or thing first, then 有 for having/presence or 無 for absence, then the thing present or absent. These verbs do not change their written form. Read the contrast: 書有帙。書無帙。 — The book has a wrapper. The book lacks a wrapper. This is not a way to negate every action.
Attempt 1. The book has its wrapper; supply “has”, not “lacks”. 書___帙。 Reference: 無 · 帙 · 異 · 破 · 字 · 有
Attempt 2. Identify which reference expression has this meaning, without following reference order: “be broken”. ___ Reference: 無 · 帙 · 異 · 破 · 字 · 有
Attempt 3. Choose the expression that means “different”, then cover the reference and write it: ___ Reference: 無 · 帙 · 異 · 破 · 字 · 有
Attempt 4. The book lacks a wrapper; supply “lacks”, not “has”. 書___帙。 Reference: 無 · 帙 · 異 · 破 · 字 · 有
Attempt 5. Read the reference in reverse order and retrieve “protective wrapper/case for a book (zhì)”: ___ Reference: 無 · 帙 · 異 · 破 · 字 · 有
Attempt 6. After a brief pause, retrieve “written character” from its meaning rather than its place in the list: ___ Reference: 無 · 帙 · 異 · 破 · 字 · 有
Check after attempting: 有 · 破 · 異 · 無 · 帙 · 字.
Chapter 2, packet 4. New forms:
葉 — yè — leaf of a book.
Attempt 1. The book has leaves; supply the word for its leaves. 書有___。 Reference: 有 · 開 · 字 · 無 · 葉 · 帙
Attempt 2. An opens the doorway; supply “open”, not “close”. 安___門。 Reference: 有 · 開 · 字 · 無 · 葉 · 帙
Attempt 3. Choose the expression that means “protective wrapper/case for a book (zhì)”, then cover the reference and write it: ___ Reference: 有 · 開 · 字 · 無 · 葉 · 帙
Attempt 4. Write the expression for “have; there is”; compare it with a different meaning in the reference. ___ Reference: 有 · 開 · 字 · 無 · 葉 · 帙
Attempt 5. Read the reference in reverse order and retrieve “written character”: ___ Reference: 有 · 開 · 字 · 無 · 葉 · 帙
Attempt 6. After a brief pause, retrieve “not have; there is no” from its meaning rather than its place in the list: ___ Reference: 有 · 開 · 字 · 無 · 葉 · 帙
Check after attempting: 葉 · 開 · 帙 · 有 · 字 · 無.
Local state contrast: 門開 means “the doorway is open”; 人開門 means “the person opens the doorway.” The first phrase describes its state here; no general passive rule is implied.
A noun immediately before another noun identifies what kind of thing is meant. These are two bounded book-material labels, not a general possessive rule.
書帙 — a book wrapper. 書葉 — a book leaf.

Worked scene (English summary follows): 安取書帙，寧視書葉。安持大書，人取小書。安開門，寧入門。 — An takes a book wrapper while Ning looks at a book leaf; An carries the large book, the person takes the small one, and An opens the doorway as Ning enters.
The same bounded noun grouping names writing by its material bearer. A short descriptive word can follow that named subject.
帙字 — writing on the wrapper. 書字 — writing in the book. 帙字少，書字多。 — The wrapper has few characters; the book has many.
Worked scene (English summary follows): 安視帙字，寧視書字。安持小書，寧持大書。人開門，安立，寧坐。 — An examines wrapper writing, Ning examines book writing, and they hold the two books as the person opens the doorway.
These two bounded quantity expressions put the amount before the character noun. They describe writing; they do not introduce a full counting-word system.
多字 — many written characters. 少字 — few written characters.
Worked scene (English summary follows): 寧有多字，安有少字。寧視大書，安開小書。人入門，安見人，寧立。 — In this new incident Ning has much writing and An little; they inspect the books before the person enters.
Keep the small book together as a unit when another noun follows it: this identifies the small book’s wrapper or leaf, rather than describing a newly measured wrapper size.
小書帙 — the small book’s wrapper. 小書葉 — a leaf of the small book. 大書葉 — a leaf of the large book.
Worked scene (English summary follows): 安持小書帙，寧視小書葉。人開大書，安視大書葉。寧持小書，安立。 — An holds the small book’s wrapper while Ning looks at its leaf; the person opens the large book and An inspects its leaves.
Extend the already learned two-book contrast only to these named materials. No broader numeral or classifier system is assumed.
二帙 — two wrappers. 二葉 — two leaves.
Worked scene (English summary follows): 安視二帙，寧持二葉。安開大書，寧閉小書。人視門，安坐，寧立。 — An looks at two wrappers and Ning holds two leaves, before they open and close the books.
A whole leaf is physically complete; a half leaf is only one part. A partly preserved written character is half a character. These expressions do not prove that two pieces join.
全葉 — a whole leaf. 半葉 — half a leaf. 半字 — half a written character.
Worked scene (English summary follows): 寧有全葉，安持半葉。人取半葉，寧視半字。安持大書，人開門。 — Ning has a whole leaf, An holds half a leaf, and a partly preserved character draws Ning’s attention.
Here a descriptive word identifies which leaf or written character is meant. Keep these three combinations bounded to their meanings; a shared character does not establish ownership.
破葉 — a damaged or torn leaf. 同字 — the same written character. 異字 — a different written character.
Worked scene (English summary follows): 安有破葉，寧有全葉。安見同字，人視異字。寧持小書，安開門。 — An has a damaged leaf and Ning a whole one; a matching character and a different character are examined.
A short comparison can describe identified names or a named pair. The comma joins only the two explicitly named things in this example.
名同。 — The names are the same. 全葉、半葉異。 — The whole leaf and the half leaf differ.

Meaning check: do matching names by themselves prove ownership? Answer: no. A matching written form is evidence to investigate. The chapter will identify whose familiar name is written, without declaring an owner.

Written-name label: 「寧」字 means “the written character 寧.” The quotation marks identify writing being examined. The same familiar graph is used in Ning’s name; the inscription does not by itself identify an owner.
